opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so mazes are a nice sandbox for us because you can actually watch the model think. With the Continuous Thought Machine, we have this internal time dimension, these "ticks" where the model keeps processing even though the input isn't changing, and we can visualize where its attention goes at each step. On a maze, you can literally see it tracing out a path, which is quite striking when you first see it.

Multiple solutions are interesting because they force a decision. If there's only one correct route, you can't really tell whether the model is reasoning or just pattern-matching toward the obvious answer. When there are several valid paths, the model has to commit to one somehow, and then the question becomes: does it stay consistent? Does it pick a route and follow it through, or does it waver between options and produce something incoherent, half of one path and half of another?

What we've found compelling is that the dynamics, the synchronization between neurons over time, seem to give it a way to hold a commitment. It explores a bit, settles, and then carries that choice forward. That feels much closer to how you or I would solve a maze: glance at the options, choose, and trace it out, backtracking if needed.

It also connects to something I care about more broadly. A lot of current models are very good at producing the single most likely answer, but real problem solving often involves a space of good answers, and you want a system that can navigate that space, not collapse to an average of it. Mazes with multiple solutions are a clean, almost toy-like way to probe that, and toy problems are often where you see the clearest signal about whether an architecture is doing something genuinely different.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that's interesting about the mazes is that when you train a standard network on them, you're not really sure what it's learned. It might have learned something like a lookup table, or some kind of shortcut, some statistical regularity in the data. And with a maze with multiple possible solutions, the model has to actually commit to one. It can't just blur over all of them. If you're doing a single feed-forward pass and there are two equally valid paths, the natural thing for a network to do is to kind of hedge, to average between them, and then you get something that isn't actually a valid path at all.

What we see with the Continuous Thought Machine is that because it has this internal temporal dimension, these ticks where it's deliberating, you can actually watch it explore. You look at the attention, and it starts at the beginning, and it kind of traces along the maze. And when it reaches a fork, you can see it sort of consider one direction and then the other, and then it picks one and follows it through. That's qualitatively really different from what you get out of a normal network. It looks like a process rather than a mapping.

And the other reason I like it is that it's a nice test of whether the model is really doing something algorithmic. We trained on mazes of a certain size, and then we gave it bigger mazes than it had ever seen, and it generalises in a way that suggests it's actually learned a procedure, something like following the path, rather than memorising patterns. Multiple-solution mazes make that much more convincing, because there isn't a single answer to memorise. The model has to be doing the search itself, and with the CTM you can actually see it doing it, which honestly is half the point of the whole thing for me. We want models where you can watch the thinking happen.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that there isn’t necessarily one correct sequence of decisions. You can take different routes and still solve the maze. So it gives us a way to ask whether the model can discover a solution, rather than just reproduce the particular path that we’ve given it as a target.

For a Continuous Thought Machine, that’s particularly interesting because it has this internal computation that unfolds over time. You can ask: what does it do with that time? Does it explore one possibility and then change its mind? Does more computation help it resolve a difficult choice?

Now, getting the right path doesn’t by itself tell you that it’s doing any of those things. But a maze gives you a fairly concrete setting in which to investigate them. You know the constraints, you can check whether a solution works, and you can allow different solutions without insisting that the model think about the problem exactly the way you would.

sol-6.1.text:
What I like about mazes is that there can be several perfectly valid routes to the goal. If you train against one particular solution, you can end up penalizing the model for finding a different route that’s equally good. What you really care about is whether it solves the maze.

For a Continuous Thought Machine, that also gives us a nice way to explore computation over time. Can it use those internal steps to work through the structure of the problem, and can giving it more time help it find a solution? The maze is easy to visualize, but it tests something more interesting than reproducing a prescribed sequence of moves.
